records.name: Vilintas
records.facts_used: Salys lists Vilintas in the Prussian branch of the Vil- name group, which he connects with viltis, “hope”. His classification preserves a Baltic name tradition while distinguishing the Prussian form from the Lithuanian examples. His Lithuanian calendar for 1964 prints Vilintas (Vilys) on 8 January. This is a dated twentieth-century calendar record of the exact name. The older Prussian classification does not by itself provide an individually dated medieval bearer.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.

records.name: Gunnar
records.facts_used: Rajandi places Gunnar in the same older Germanic family as Gunther and Günther, distinguishing its Scandinavian and German forms. He connects the family with saga and Nibelungen traditions, without treating literary characters as Estonian birth records. In his account of use around 1962, Gunnar is the more frequent spelling and Kunnar the rarer one, approximately nine to one. This is a historical comparison in a 1966 book, not a current population count and not the first appearance of either form.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: PDF 67 / printed 69: shared Gunnar/Kunnar history, 1962 frequency. Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Kunder
records.facts_used: Rajandi associates Kunder with the German branch of the Gunnar/Gunther family and also records Kunter. He distinguishes the form’s earlier given-name use from its continued occurrence as a surname. He finds Kunder/Kunter among fathers’ given names in Tallinn records of 1961–1962. This is evidence from the fathers’ generation. It cannot be reported as the number of babies named Kunder during those years.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
